GPT-6 Pro finds supposed errors in academic papers all the time, just as part of other work. Confirming the errors & learning their importance would still take a lot of time today, but it will get faster. We don't have the right mechanisms in place to deal a flood of corrections.

I suspect the vast majority of these are nitpicks, so I wouldn't assume that they overturn results and papers. They don't fall into the normal corrections process, making it hard to understand how to handle them well within the constraints of academic publishing.

Ben Affleck, the actor who also runs Artists Equity, walks through his method for fine-tuning open video models: unfreeze the weights, then train only the final cinematic layer, so the output meets the standard a real film crew works to. Some background: in 2022 he started InterPositive, a 16-person AI company for film post-production. Netflix acquired it in March 2026 for $587M, all cash. Why build it at all? The public video models had learned from his colleagues' films, and he didn't see a real business in that. So InterPositive raised money, spent 8 months filming its own dataset on a controlled stage, and used that footage only for late-stage training. From there, every new film trains its own private model on its own dailies. The production keeps both the footage and what the model learned from it. That is what Netflix paid $587 million for. I'd love to share a blog post with you explaining the research agenda of the Commission of Artificial Intelligence and the Future of the American Workforce. My own focus will be on the impact of AI on Technology Industry - what AI can do today and what we can expect it to do in the near future. Other researchers on the commission and their specific focus are: - Bill Congdon will explore several scenarios of how AI could change the US labor market and affect workers - John Soroushian will explore how AI is currently being regulated and identify the policy levers that can effectively guide the pace and direction of AI adoption - Adam Leonard will lead research on the reforms needed to federal, state, and private data systems. - Kevin Corinth will identify the programs that could provide a cushion for workers as they transition between jobs and industries - Brent Parton will work to understand how to fund and design training and reskilling programs - Jason Tyszko will examine real-time changes in employers’ talent needs and how policymakers can protect jobs and workers - Rekha Balu will lead research on how AI’s effects may vary across regions and localities. You can read more about all these efforts in the following post: https://aiworkforcecommission.org/latest/ai-research-agenda-adapted-uncertainty

New paper from Microsoft and colleagues on generating enterprise data for agents. If you train or evaluate agents on long-running business work, it's worth your time. (bookmark it) MiniCorp is an office simulator. A firm of agents runs an e-commerce company, discusses decisions in messages and meetings, and sets prices, inventory, and ad spend. A simulated market with customers and adaptive competitors responds, and the firm reacts to the results. The market is checked against published studies of real ones. A four-week 20% discount lifts units by 71%, and sales stay 31% above control after prices return to normal. Checkpoints let the same market state replay with a different decision, giving paired outcomes that real company records cannot provide. Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05912 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/minicorp-the-last-mile-of-the-ai-agent-firm-2610.05912

Must-read paper on the effectiveness of multi-agent systems and persistent memory. We have recently seen many viral examples of multi-agent systems scaled via persistent memory. This work takes a closer look. They test one three-tier chain-of-agents system. Splitting long-context work across agents cuts peak KV cache to 14.3 MiB per query, against about 35 MiB for single-pass and RAG baselines. The persistent trace-recall tier adds 0.368 MiB of peak cache and changes accuracy by +0.015, with a confidence interval that crosses zero. The authors explain why. Single-question benchmarks give each item its own evidence and score it independently, so stored traces have nothing useful to recall. Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07782 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/persistent-memory-in-multi-agent-llm-inference-what-it-costs-what-it-buys-and-wh-2610.07782

When China figures out how to manufacture a product, their ability to scale is often greater than the rest of the world combined. We saw this with lithium batteries and solar, for example. SpaceX is a rare counter-example, where its mass to orbit is roughly an order of magnitude greater than the rest of the world, BUT China now does a majority of non-SpaceX mass to orbit. SpaceX is an anomaly in the matrix. Maybe RAM will be different, but RAM was a low margin commodity only ~3 years ago. LP5 and LP6 are designed to a common standard that China seems to be solving fast. Newer HBM architectures and things like an SRAM layer below logic and 3D stacking RAM on top of logic while finding a way to keep the logic cooled will be harder to solve.

Every email marketer has sat in this exact meeting. Two versions on the screen. Everyone has an opinion. Someone says let's just test it. You split the list, send both, and one wins by 6%. Slack gets a green tick. Nice, version B it is. Everyone moves on. Nobody ever says the obvious part out loud: A 6% win means almost half your list just got the worse email. And you'll run it again next week. @getallanai is the first thing I've seen that gets you out of that loop. It sits on top of Omnisend and Klaviyo. Your designer uploads blocks instead of finished emails, or you let Allan's AI generate assets for you. Allan assembles a different email for each subscriber and learns what that person responds to. Nobody gets handed the version they didn't want. I spent years getting good at picking. I'd rather not have to. See it for yourself → https://getallan.com/?utm_source=chase

Before you spend another dollar on ads, run your welcome emails through this prompt. Every subscriber your ads bring in gets these emails first. Paste this into ChatGPT or Claude, then add your popup and your emails at the bottom: "Audit my ecommerce welcome email series. Below I'll paste my signup popup (the offer and any question it asks), whether the series stops when someone buys, and every welcome email in order with its subject line, preview text, send delay, buttons, and body copy. If you can, also attach a phone screenshot of each email. Check it against these rules: 1. Email 1 sends right after signup, with no delay. 2. The promised code or offer is in the first lines of email 1, before any brand story. 3. The series has 5 to 7 emails spread over 10 to 14 days. 4. Across the series, it covers why the brand started, the problem the product solves, how it solves it, one specific customer review, and the biggest reason people hesitate (price, fit, quality, or shipping). 5. Each email asks for one action. Several buttons are fine if they all go to the same place. 6. If my popup asks a question, later emails use the answer. If it doesn't, an early email asks what they're shopping for. 7. If the offer expires, the last email gives the exact date and time. 8. The series stops once someone buys. 9. Each subject line makes clear what's inside, and the preview text adds to it instead of repeating it or showing filler like "View in browser." 10. If I attached screenshots, check each email on mobile: the offer and main button show without scrolling, the text is easy to read, and it doesn't rely on one big image. Then give me: 1. Every fix, ranked by how much it likely affects sales. For each one, quote the line from my email that has the problem, say why it matters in one sentence, and give the fix. 2. Rewrites I can paste for the top 3 fixes, in my brand's voice. Don't make up reviews, numbers, or facts about my brand. Use [brackets] for anything I need to fill in. 3. Any rule you couldn't check from what I pasted. My popup: [paste] Does the series stop when someone buys?
